To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the dynamical evolution of planetary systems is a rich and complex field of research, that the dynamical processes of migration and resonant capture are not fully understood, that there is a critical planetary mass above which the planetary system is unstable and below which the system is stable, and that the dynamical excitation of planetary systems is not fully understood.
the dynamical evolution of compact multiplanet systems is strongly influenced by the resonant interactions between the planets, which can lead to instability and planet-planet collisions.

In summary, our research is concerned with
resonant dynamics of planetary systems.
the dynamical resonances in extrasolar planetary systems and in particular with the resonances of mean motion in systems of super-Earths.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
resonant chains of planets are unstable, but they can survive for billions of years, which may explain the lack of observed resonant chains of exoplanets.

, in the context of the migration scenario, the lack of resonance chains in the observed systems is not in contradiction with the formation of resonance chains in protoplanetary disks, if the post-disk instability phase is very common.
the dynamical history of planetary systems is a combination of resonant and dissipative processes that are not necessarily exclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how the dynamical evolution of planetary systems is affected by resonances.

the observed architecture of exoplanetary systems is compatible with the dynamical scenario of resonant capture followed by dissipative evolution, provided that the system is initially unstable after the disappearance of the disk, and that the system becomes stabilized by the dissipative process.
the dynamical history of the planetary systems is crucial in order to understand their observed architecture, and the resonant dynamics is a key ingredient to describe their evolution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the observed distribution of the orbital periods of super-Earths is not compatible with the standard model of planet formation and migration in a gaseous protoplanetary disk.
the dynamical history of a planetary system can have a profound impact on the architecture of the system, and on the orbital properties of the planets.
resonant chains of super-Earths are unstable, and that this instability is more common in systems that are more compact and populated with heavier planets.
